meaning: Each tie names the phrase of the paper that a Lean declaration states, as read side by side for Proof Reader (wcook04/proof-reader 3858afbe00b2, papers/navier-stokes-index). Titles, reading notes, topics and comparisons are AI-drafted or AI-assessed; no mathematician has reviewed them.

families.name: From a certificate to a profile
From cell data to the certificate

topics.name: The blow-up statements
topics.description: Smooth solutions, breakdown on space and on the torus, and the theorems that state them (Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1).

topics.name: The fractional extension
topics.description: The authors' separate extension with dissipation exponent between 1 and 5/4, outside the classical paper.

topics.name: Heat flow and mild solutions
topics.description: The heat semigroup, the bilinear Duhamel term, mild solutions, restarting and uniqueness (§3).

topics.name: Recurrent profiles
topics.description: Self-similar time-periodic profiles, their slices and orbits, and weak profiles read as physical fields (§2, §4.1, §7.11).

topics.name: Monodromy and the correction
topics.description: The period map, its compact-plus-small splitting, the spectral projection and the fixed point that corrects a profile to an exact solution (§4).

topics.name: Passing to the torus
topics.description: The solenoidal cutoff, periodization and the periodic right inverse that move the construction onto the torus (§5–6).

topics.name: From certificate to profile
topics.description: Certificate data, the free operator, convection, held solutions and the smoothing of the weak profile they produce (§7).

topics.name: The coercive multiplier estimate
topics.description: The multiplier, its five density coefficients and lower bound, and the a priori estimate it gives (Appendix B.1 and B.2).

topics.name: Encoded cell data
topics.description: The finitely represented inputs: coordinates and harmonics, the profile representation, splines and jets, physical cells, rows, weights and potentials.

topics.name: Reduction to the quarter plane
topics.description: Symmetry reduction of the density to the meridian quarter plane (B.3).

topics.name: Cells, traces and tails
topics.description: Integrability, the common vector of unknowns, resolved modes, the tail budget and the exterior estimate (B.4).

topics.name: Angular and ray-exterior tests
topics.description: The angular inequalities, the pointwise test and the integrated test on ray exteriors (B.5 and B.6).

topics.name: The matrix tree lower bound
topics.description: The tree conditions on the cell matrices and the passage from all cells to the global inequality (B.7 and B.8).

topics.name: Changing the profile
topics.description: Bounds for moving estimates from the reference field to the actual profile (B.9).

topics.name: The adjoint pairing and its error
topics.description: The quadratic adjoint pairing, the azimuthal dual norm and the linear adjoint error with potentials and pins (B.10 to B.12).

topics.name: The offset and the certificate
topics.description: Enclosing the constant, linear and quadratic offset, and the fifteen fields of CellSystemCondition that make the data a certificate (B.13 and B.14).

notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt: The sum includes the potential budget, possible fitted-direction budgets and the free parameter and time-shift budgets. Setting the fitted set empty and adding the separate pin charge gives the three-part expression (B.53).
The flux is ∇ψ−ΣYⱼₗ(∇Φ̃ₗ−∇Φ̃ₗᵀ). For divergence-free generators its negative divergence gives −∆ψ+ΣYⱼₗ∆Φ̃ₗ, identifying the corresponding terms of (B.52).
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalBounded: The harmonic part has distinct component, time-frequency and azimuthal-frequency triples and the weighted sum with denominator (|k|+1/2)². This is exactly the improved harmonic budget in the definition preceding Lemma B.11.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti: The identity assumes L² matrix columns and |y| times their divergence in L². The paper states (B.55) for matrix fields with divergence in L⁶ᐟ⁵; these are different sufficient hypotheses, and the formal argument uses the weighted Hardy bound.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsPotentialData: The potential assumptions add |U|≲(1+|y|)⁻¹ and require bounded-near-origin Laplacians with decay (1+|y|)⁻⁴ for G and (1+|y|)⁻³ for U. These imply the coarser common derivative bound (B.51), after increasing its unspecified constant.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointDefectBri: The theorem combines the potential, parameter and pin estimates after decomposing the adjoint pairing. It concludes the absolute bound (7.33); the raw three-line equality (B.56) is established through separate identities inside that argument.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.remainderField: The residual combines the adjoint transport, negative divergence of the pin flux, ∇q, ∆G+w*∆U and −div Fᵀ. With divergence-free pin generators and the stated transpose convention, this is (B.52).
notes.Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.heightRat: For y≠0 the polar coordinate is y₃/|y|. A value is also assigned at y=0, where the polar coordinate in the paper is undefined; none of the geometric formulas needs that point.
notes.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CellSystemCond: The fifteen groups of assumptions include multiplier bounds, pointwise cell inequalities, matrix comparisons, and profile, potential, adjoint and offset conditions. They supply the full hypothesis of the certificate construction, including the requirements omitted after Proposition B.14; their satisfaction by concrete data remains an assumption.
notes.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isExtendedCert: The construction produces a certificate after choosing a sufficiently large decay constant, from the full fifteen groups of cell assumptions and the analytic estimates. The paper omits some finite-data hypotheses, so equivalence of the complete condition lists cannot be checked from Proposition B.14 alone.
notes.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.spaceBreakdown: The conclusion is whole-space nonexistence of a global smooth solution with uniformly bounded energy, obtained by composing the cell and profile implications. Proposition B.14 itself concludes that the data form a certificate; the existence of valid concrete data remains an assumption here.
notes.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is: The profile representation is linked to its derivatives and to pinning values, with the target chosen to equal the approximate profile's pinning values. Consequently the correction has the zero pinning gap prescribed in Appendix B; the general certificate of Section 7 allows other gaps.
notes.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.ce: The constant residual has the similarity drift, diffusion, central advection, actuator force and ∇(q⁰−|W₀⁰|²/2). These are exactly F⁽⁰⁾ in (B.57).
notes.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.li: The linear residual includes the period derivative ςᵢ∂θW₀⁰, both mixed advections, the tangent actuator force and ∇(qⁱ−W₀⁰·W₀ⁱ). This is F⁽ⁱ⁾ in (B.57).
The theorem constructs a continuous periodic energy-space representative of the free solution and its similarity-time integrated energy identity.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.Internal.FreePerturbation: The free similarity equation is verified by differentiating its pairing with smooth compactly supported test fields.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.bordered: The unknown is f = T_Sv; applying the free inverse recovers v before convection and the constraints are evaluated.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.extendedDataContinuityHol: Continuity is proved after testing the residual against solenoidal fields. No continuity of the unprojected residual in H is assumed.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.extendedFrozenBridgeHolds: The lower bound at the approximate profile is obtained by adding the reference-profile lower bound and the allowed shift of the quadratic form.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.freeEnergyLocalHolds_of: The energy identity is integrated over time intervals for a continuous periodic scalar energy. The physical-time identity (7.45) is related by the similarity change of variables.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.productBoundHolds_of: The estimate allows different first and second factors, using the weighted norm of the first and the gradient supremum of the second.
notes.Breakdown.Cert.sizeZ: At this stage ω has been reduced to one by rescaling the forcing fields and their coefficients.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.EliminationC: The cell-matrix comparison is imposed on the allowed local vectors, with further eliminated-mode and row-matrix conditions. Identifying that set with the vectors XQxg also uses the pressure-gauge and compatibility conditions omitted from the paper.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.InRowRange: A compatible local vector is a global row value plus pressure-gauge and constant-pressure directions, with real forcing and pinning coordinates. This is more explicit than the paper's notation x=XQxg, and the equivalence uses the additional gauge-invariance conditions.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.Internal.ModeT: The gradient-coefficient reflection identity is proved for y₃≠0. This is sufficient for the integrated symmetry argument, while the printed (B.17) is written without the pointwise restriction.
The curl-coefficient reflection identity is proved for y₃≠0. The printed (B.17) gives no such exclusion; the excluded plane has zero measure for the density integrals.
The velocity-coefficient reflection identity is proved for y₃≠0. The restriction leaves the integral unchanged but is narrower than the unrestricted pointwise wording of (B.17).
The curl-gradient allocation is invariant under the reflected label and point when y₃≠0. The printed coefficient identity does not state this restriction.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.IsFlipCompatib: The weight and harmonic reflection conditions are explicit, while reflection of the auxiliary piecewise constant functions is required only off y₃=0. Thus the complete pointwise hypothesis differs from the unrestricted wording preceding (B.17).
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.IsModeClass: The two required symmetries are the half-period twist by π/κ and the half-turn about the first axis. The auxiliary condition allows κ≥1; the cell assumptions impose the paper's κ≥3.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.modeFlip: The reflected velocity-mode identity is proved almost everywhere for weak perturbations, together with the corresponding gradient and Hessian identities. The velocity clause is (B.24), interpreted in the weak-function setting of the surrounding argument.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.modeShiftRotat: For periodic fields whose orbital integral exists, a time shift and axial rotation multiply the projected mode by its harmonic and rotate its vector value. This is (B.13), with the integrability needed for the change of variables stated explicitly.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.modeTermFlip: The density reflection identity follows from the coefficient and derivative reflection identities at points with y₃≠0. It provides the almost-everywhere equality needed in the integrals, with a pointwise restriction absent from (B.17).
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsCellFo: The local inequality uses explicit row, pairing, strain-slack and credit contributions and separates the positive and negative integrals. It serves the role of (B.33), with a specified symmetric pressure gradient and without the paper's four existential error variables.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.CellHypothesis: The full cell assumptions include κ≥3 and the constants w*=39/50, c=3/50, pinning weight 1000 and row cap 400(1+2⁻¹⁸). They also require the cell, matrix, pressure and error conditions described, and partly omitted, in Appendix B.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.field: The cell tensor has the same harmonic and reflection construction as Ξᵢ, with matrix indices ordered as output then derivative direction. Transposing the paper's derivative-first convention identifies the same pairing in (B.10).
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesCom: The complex-node condition includes the two comparisons and weighted residual test, together with the permitted complex coordinates, scale, pivot bounds and real and imaginary negative columns. These are the additional conditions described after (B.40).
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel: These are the conjugation, reflection, spline joining, vanishing and exponent conditions around (B.6)–(B.8). They specify admissible coefficients; the vector-field formula itself is supplied separately.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.reducedCom: The nonzero azimuthal mode uses the factors σʰ⁰(1−σ)ʰ(1−η²)² and division by κι₁ to enforce zero divergence. The zero azimuthal mode uses the stream and swirl formulas of (B.8).
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.shapeInfoF: The represented field is the real part of the finite vector-harmonic sum, as printed in (B.6). Conjugation, reflection and spline matching are required separately.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.GeneratedByC: Every allowed symmetry is a power of the axial twist, possibly followed by the half-turn, with an integer time translation. This is the restriction on Γ stated after (B.1).
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.ModeCoefficients.ofPi: The five cell coefficients include the leading terms printed below (B.16) and the full multiplier corrections. The paper explicitly leaves those corrections unwritten, so their complete formulas cannot be compared term by term with the manuscript.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.RowValues.mix: For positive definite Gram data the mixing matrix is G⁻¹ᐟ². The factor √τₖ is applied through the separate row weight when the row seminorm is formed.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.RowValues.rowFieldOf: The formal row fields have unit norm after multiplication by G⁻¹ᐟ². The paper includes √τₖ in eₖ itself; the same seminorm is recovered by multiplying the squared formal row pairing by τₖ.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.RowValues.rowWeightOf: The row weight is the cell test weight divided by c; at c=3/50 it is τₖ. The paper places √τₖ in the field eₖ, whereas the formal row seminorm carries τₖ as a separate weight.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsDirectionR: The directional radius is measurable, homogeneous of degree zero, uniformly positive and bounded above. The paper allows dependence on direction without spelling out these uniform bounds.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.TailBudget.H: The complete absorption condition bounds the sum of gradient, potential, leakage and velocity-tail charges by I₂ times the gain in (B.27). The printed expression specifies the available threshold, without listing every charge in this condition.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.initialState_closed: The global estimate already uses 2ζ·ℓ−|ζ|²/1000≤1000|ℓ|². It therefore bounds the assembled form by the final density gap, while (B.44) still displays the uncompleted pinning square.
notes.Breakdown.CertCell.labelPhase: The harmonic is exp(i[2π(2ι₂−ι₁)θ+κι₁φ]), with the same signs and integer frequencies as (B.2).
notes.Breakdown.CertReduction.EnergyBoundsHold: The combined assertion consists of spatial supremum and period energy estimates at constant weight. The paper's (B.46) is a four-part spatial statement assuming only a lower bound for a possibly variable weight.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.IsAdmissibleWeak: Admissibility includes positive c,cμ<1, a positive period and lower weight, regularity and decay, transport and harmonic bounds, one-sided frequencies and all auxiliary losses. The paper describes several of these requirements without writing their complete formulas.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.PieceMultiplierDe: This is the full multiplier assertion for weak perturbations, with positive and negative density integrals kept separate. It yields the real signed inequality of Proposition B.1 once the negative part is finite and the full coefficient assumptions hold.
notes.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.RowRestClause: The condition states finiteness of negative density and the lower bound (B.21), with c and the pinning weight as parameters. Taking c=3/50 and the pinning weight 1000 gives the printed constants, after subtracting the finite negative integral.
notes.Breakdown.DichotomyHolds: For a compact perturbation of an operator of norm at most b≤α<β, the spectral conclusion gives a commuting finite-rank projection and geometric bounds with α<r₁<r₂<β, together with surjectivity on the exceptional range. Taking α=b=exp(−S/4), β=1 and r₁<Θ<r₂ gives the two convergent series in (4.11).
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.IsHeld: A fixed-parameter correction must satisfy the equation, constraints, weighted radius and essential gradient-supremum bound.
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.defect: A weak Hessian and a pressure-gradient representative are selected when the residual field is formed.
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.params: Intervals constrain the adjoint coordinates; a scaled Euclidean ball constrains the complementary coordinates.
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.target: Subtract the approximate profile’s constraint from the complete-field target to obtain the prescribed correction target ℓ̄(α).
notes.Breakdown.FarField.farFieldDecay_holds: Weighted estimates for the profile integral equation give velocity derivatives through order two and pressure-gradient decay.
notes.Breakdown.FarField.periodicLerayProfileE: The input and output assert existence. The conclusion does not preserve an equality with a specified original weak field.
notes.Breakdown.FarField.smoothFieldOfOrbit_ho: The smooth velocity preserves the chosen mild orbit at every time, with equality almost everywhere in space.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.BilinCompact: For positive heat time, the operator in the second input is compact when its first input is a compact smooth solenoidal field in the dense test class. Lemma 3.2 allows every first input in X; extending to that class uses density and continuity in operator norm.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.IsWeakSolution: The weak momentum identity is imposed at interior times against compact solenoidal test fields, with diffusion written by the gradient pairing and transport by the advection pairing. The full assumptions also require smooth decaying slices, continuity in X, L²-continuous differences between slices, and continuity of test pairings at the endpoints.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.bilinX: The bilinear operator on X is specified by its dual trilinear pairing, with the transport formula then proved on a dense compact test class. Display (2.3) defines it through projected heat evolution for all inputs in X.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.heatDivFree: The projected heat map takes L² forcing into the gradient-weighted Fourier realization of X. The formula in (2.2) is stated on the larger class L¹+L².
notes.Breakdown.Freq.heat_holds: The heat flow is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup from time zero, is self-adjoint, and agrees with its Gaussian Fourier multiplier. Its realization on X supplies (3.3).
notes.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: The heat operators form a strongly continuous contraction semigroup, and the symmetric bilinear kernel commutes with forward heat shifts. Its τ⁻³⁄⁴ bound is required only for 0<τ≤1, whereas (3.12) requires that bound for every τ>0.
notes.Breakdown.Held.testSetZero_of: The proof forms the simplified Newton update and uses the two enclosures to keep it in K; a fixed point then has zero total force.
notes.Breakdown.IsPerturbation: The drift-time field is S⁻¹∂_θv + ½v + ½(y·∇)v. The Laplacian is subtracted separately in the equation.
notes.Breakdown.IsRightSide: The relation is equality of integrals against all smooth compactly supported solenoidal space-time tests.
notes.Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile: The velocity and pressure solve the smooth similarity equation, with |∇ʲW| ≤ C(1+|y|)⁻¹⁻ʲ for j=0,1,2 and |∇q| ≤ C(1+|y|)⁻³. Periodicity and nonvanishing are separate assumptions when this local profile condition is used.
notes.Breakdown.IsSmoothSolution: The velocity and pressure are smooth on nonnegative times, the prescribed initial velocity is attained, and the momentum equation and zero divergence hold at positive times. Setting the viscosity to one gives (1.1).
notes.Breakdown.MildFramework: The assumptions require the short-time bilinear bound with exponent −3/4, the heat and dilation identities, and compactness when one bilinear input ranges over a dense set. Rotation compatibility is imposed separately in the physical realization.
notes.Breakdown.MildFramework.IsOrbit: A continuous nonzero energy-space curve has positive period P, obeys w(s+P)=ρw(s), and solves the similarity-time integral equation. The physical-time identities (1.5) and (4.2) require the change of variables and dilation as well.
notes.Breakdown.MildRegular: From compact smooth solenoidal initial data, a mild curve on [0,T] has smooth velocity and pressure representatives, with bounded kinetic energy and gradient norm on that interval. Lemma 2.3 additionally states energy nonincrease throughout the lifespan and a periodic assertion.
notes.Breakdown.MonodromyStatement: After sufficiently short intervals are composed and the twist removed, the period map differs compactly from the free product, whose norm is at most exp(−P/4). The same statement also provides inverses of the short-interval operators with norm at most 4/3.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.HeatDivFreeComparison: Compactly supported L² forcing has arbitrarily small local projected-heat discrepancy, measured by δ times its L³⁄² norm, at sufficiently small scale and on a compact positive-time window. Lemma 6.1 gives an all-time CL⁻⁷⁄² estimate for the divergence of a W¹,¹ tensor, in terms of that tensor’s L¹ norm.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.KernelSharpBound: The bilinear smoothing bound is Cτ⁻³⁄⁴ in the inhomogeneous unit-torus norm, for 0<τ≤1. Lemma 3.7 and (3.20) use mean-zero homogeneous spaces at every spatial period and all positive times.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup: The conclusion supplies a smooth periodic solenoidal datum and a mild trajectory whose inhomogeneous H¹ norm is unbounded on [0,T), for some T>0. Proposition 2.2 additionally gives T≤1, the two-sided rate, and local convergence to the profile.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.TransplantNorm: The rescaled transplant has squared norm ∫|∇g|²+μ∫|g|² because the unit-torus norm is inhomogeneous. The equality in (6.1) concerns the homogeneous gradient norm, preserved by unscaled periodization.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.V: The unit-torus Fourier norm uses 1+4π²|k|² and permits the zero mode. Displays (3.15) and (3.16) concern the homogeneous gradient norm on mean-zero fields, with a separate equivalence to H¹ at period one.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.trigHs: Finite Fourier polynomials on the unit cell satisfy an L⁶ estimate using the weight 1+4π²|k|². Display (3.18) is the homogeneous Sobolev inequality for all mean-zero fields, uniformly over every period; (3.19) is a separate heat-forcing estimate.
notes.Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist: A smooth nonzero profile has a positive period and an orthogonal twist, solves the similarity equation, and satisfies uniform bounds |∇ʲW| ≤ C(1+|y|)⁻¹⁻ʲ for j=0,1,2 and |∇q| ≤ C(1+|y|)⁻³. The second-derivative and pressure-gradient bounds are additional written hypotheses beyond (1.3).
notes.Breakdown.PieceWeights.IsMultiplierField: The multiplier is characterized by the test pairing in (B.14), with finite L² norm, time periodicity and zero pairing against pressure gradients. These are the stated requirements that Mv belong to Hdiv.
notes.Breakdown.PotentialShape.IsPotentialSeri: The condition imposes polynomial joining, axis behavior and endpoint decay for the finite potential series. The paper explicitly does not print that representation, so this condition cannot be identified with the displayed analytic bounds (B.51) alone.
notes.Breakdown.Realization: The physical representation preserves the gradient norm, nonvanishing, rotations and dilations. It also converts the stated distributional evolution into a mild solution and supplies dense smooth compactly supported solenoidal data.
notes.Breakdown.TransferHolds: For every prescribed dense class of initial data and every ε>0, the formal conclusion chooses one mild solution whose datum is within ε of W(0) and whose dilated error is at most C(1−t)^κ for some κ>0. Proposition 2.1 also chooses a fixed finite-dimensional correction space and treats every sufficiently close datum; that whole family is absent from this conclusion.
notes.Breakdown.WeakProfile.physicalCurve: The formula uses s = s₀ − log(1−t) and dilation by 1/(1−t); conversion from normalized time θ to s has already occurred.
notes.Breakdown.WeakProfile.physicalIdentity_o: The theorem transforms the weak nonlinear equation after testing. The paper also interprets the separate free-operator identities (7.41) distributionally.
notes.Breakdown.extended_certificate_orbit_pro: The proof assembles the analytic implications, while its conclusion retains only existence of a weak profile. The parameter and quantitative bounds are not part of that conclusion.
notes.Breakdown.physicalField: The physical curve is D_{(1−t)⁻¹}W(s₀−log(1−t)), with final time fixed to one and arbitrary phase s₀. Display (1.4) allows any positive final time T.
notes.Breakdown.rowNorm: The weights of orthonormal row fields can be absorbed into the fields to recover the paper’s orthogonal family.
notes.Breakdown.sigmaSimilarityIntegrand: Solenoidal tests remove pressure, and integration by parts transfers the derivatives to the test field.

lean.fidelity_note: The vanishing residual is ∂ₛW+W/2+(y·∇)W/2−ΔW+(W·∇)W+∇q=0, the momentum equation of (1.2). This expression contains neither the divergence condition nor the twisted recurrence in the rest of that display.

lean.name: Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExists
lean.fidelity_note: The premise includes the similarity equation, zero divergence and recurrence W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R⁻¹y) from (1.2).
